summary: Describes the PPP Serial Data Transport Protocol, a network-level protocol for PPP that carries serial data streams over a PPP link, with its own control protocol. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A pipe inside a pipe: it lets an old-fashioned serial connection ride along inside a modern PPP link.

subtitle: Transporting serial data streams over PPP with optional compression.

tldr.problem: Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) was designed for multi-protocol network datagrams, but some applications need to send serial data (like HDLC-like synchronous or asynchronous data) over PPP links. Without a way to encapsulate and control serial data, applications cannot leverage PPP's compression features for serial streams.
tldr.mechanism: PPP Serial Data Transport Protocol (SDTP) defines an encapsulation format based on ITU-T Recommendation V.120, which includes a header carrying frame status information. Paired with the Serial Data Control Protocol (SDCP), it allows negotiation of options like frame format, port multiplexing, and maximum frame size.
tldr.outcome: Serial data can be transported over PPP links and combined with PPP compression protocols to provide synchronous data compression. The protocol was developed for use in DSU/CSUs (data service units) and similar equipment.

today: RFC 1963 is an Informational document describing a protocol for transporting serial data over PPP. It has not been adopted as a standards track specification and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
PPP Serial Data Transport Protocol (SDTP) provides a way to encapsulate and transport serial data streams over PPP links. The protocol was developed to allow PPP's existing compression features to be used for synchronous data compression.

SDTP defines the encapsulation of serial data and is paired with PPP Serial Data Control Protocol (SDCP), which handles configuration and negotiation between the two ends of the link. The two protocols together enable features such as synchronous data compression, multi-port multiplexing, and support for both HDLC-like synchronous and asynchronous serial data.

The protocol uses a terminal adaptation header based on ITU-T Recommendation V.120, with optional extensions for port numbers, length fields, and control state information. The default packet format is designed to work efficiently with PPP compression protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP SDTP is a way to send old-style serial data through modern PPP networks. It combines PPP's compression features with serial data so you can squeeze old data formats through fast networks.

sections.title: Packet Format and Structure
sections.content:
Before SDTP can operate, the PPP link must reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase and the SDTP Control Protocol must open successfully.

By default, one SDTP packet is placed in each PPP frame. The packet includes a PPP Protocol ID (0x0049) and may include several optional fields: a Length field, a Port field, a Header field, the transported data, and optional padding.

The packet format has two variants: Header-Last (default), where the header appears after the data with its octets reversed, and Header-First, where the header precedes the data. The Header-Last format is optimized for use with compression, allowing the decision to compress the header to be made after observing the packet's compressed size.

The Header field is the V.120 terminal adaptation header, containing one or two octets with bits indicating frame boundaries (Begin, Final), error status (C1, C2), break conditions, and flow control.
sections.plainLanguage: A serial data packet looks like a numbered envelope with the address sometimes at the end and sometimes at the start, depending on how it is configured.

sections.title: The V.120 Terminal Adaptation Header
sections.content:
The first octet of the Header field is the V.120 Terminal Adaptation Header. It contains eight bits with specific meanings:

E (Extension): Set to 0 if a Control State Information octet follows; set to 1 if this is the final header octet.

BR (Break/HDLC Idle): In asynchronous mode, indicates a BREAK signal. In synchronous mode, indicates HDLC idle.

FC (Flow Control): Used to signal Flow-Off (receiver not ready) or Flow-On (receiver ready). Flow-Off messages expire after a configurable timeout to prevent hangups.

C1, C2 (Error Control): Indicate error conditions such as FCS errors, abort conditions, parity errors, or overrun.

B, F (Segmentation): Indicate frame boundaries. B=1 marks the beginning, F=1 marks the final portion. For asynchronous mode, both must be 1.

An optional second octet carries Control State Information, indicating if the DTE port is activated, ready to send, and ready to receive.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is like a post-it note on each chunk of serial data, saying whether it is the start, middle, or end of a message, and whether there are any problems or the receiver is ready.

sections.title: Configuration and Control
sections.content:
PPP Serial Data Control Protocol (SDCP) is responsible for configuring and enabling SDTP modules on both ends of a link. SDCP is based on the PPP Link Control Protocol (LCP) and uses the same packet exchange and state machine mechanism.

SDCP negotiates several options:

Packet-Format selects Header-Last (default) or Header-First layout.

Header-Type specifies whether the Header field includes only the first octet (H-Only) or may include an optional Control State Information octet (H-and-CS or H-and-CS-Always).

Length-Field-Present enables a length field in each packet, allowing multiple SDTP packets in a single PPP frame.

Multi-Port enables a port number field for multiplexing multiple serial streams on a single PPP link.

Transport-Mode specifies HDLC Synchronous (default) or Asynchronous operation for a given port.

Additional options configure maximum frame size, FCS handling, and flow-control expiration time.
sections.plainLanguage: SDCP is the negotiation part where the two routers agree on exactly how to format and handle the serial data before they start sending it.

sections.title: Key Features and Modes
sections.content:
Frame Segmentation: The B and F bits in the header allow a single serial data frame to be split across multiple SDTP packets. This is useful when working with compression, as it allows a large frame to be segmented before compression is applied.

Flow Control: The FC bit can be used to signal that the receiver is not ready (Flow-Off). A Flow-Off expires after a configured time (default 10 seconds), so the sender can resume transmitting if an acknowledgment is missed.

Non-Octet-Aligned Frames: For applications using non-octet-aligned HDLC frames, an optional Odd-Pad field can be negotiated to align frames to octet boundaries.

Error Signaling: The C1 and C2 bits carry error information from the DTE port, such as FCS errors, abort conditions, or parity errors, allowing the remote end to handle errors appropriately.

Multi-Port Multiplexing: When the Multi-Port option is negotiated, a port number field allows multiple serial data streams to be multiplexed over a single PPP link.
sections.plainLanguage: SDTP can break big messages into pieces, pause and resume if needed, handle errors, and carry multiple independent streams all at once.
